title: Muchukunda asks for nothing
hookLine: an army at the gate, Krishna runs into a cave, and an old king inside is offered anything
tomorrow: what does a princess do when she's promised to the wrong man?

cards: Mathura has no peace. Jarasandha, the powerful king whose daughters were married to Kamsa, attacks the city again and again. Krishna turns his armies back each time, and each time Jarasandha returns.
Now a second enemy marches on the city too, a fierce king called Kalayavana, with a vast army. Two forces, one city. And the Bhagavata gives its hero a strange move.
Krishna walks out through the city gate, alone, without a weapon, wearing a garland, and lets the enemy king see him. Then he turns and runs.

teach.h: FIRST, A CITY IN THE SEA.
teach.b: First, he protects his people. Before he steps outside, Krishna has a new city built in the sea, Dwaraka, and the text says he moves the people of Mathura there by his own power, so they wake up somewhere safe.
Only then does he walk out. Kalayavana recognizes him from what he's heard and, being proud, chases him on foot, man to man.
Krishna stays just out of reach, up into the hills and into a mountain cave. Kalayavana charges in and sees a man lying asleep. Thinking it's Krishna, he kicks him.

The sleeper is Muchukunda, an ancient king who once fought for the gods and asked them, as his reward, for sleep. He wakes, looks at the man who kicked him, and the text says that at his glance Kalayavana burns to ashes.
Then Krishna shows himself, and here is the heart of the chapter.
Krishna offers the old king any boon he likes. Muchukunda says no. In paraphrase: I spent my life chasing kingdoms and pride, and it was a trap; now I want nothing but shelter at your feet.
And Krishna is pleased that the offer didn't tempt him. That's the Bhagavata's picture of the highest devotion: loving God for God, not for what God can give.
Hindus pray for things all the time, health, a child, an exam, and the Gita calls those who come asking noble too.
But the devotee these stories hold up is the one who asks for God himself. And the runaway? Gujarat still loves Krishna as Ranchhod, explained by devotees as the one who left the battlefield.
There, it's a title of love.

how: In parts of Gujarat, Krishna is worshipped as Ranchhod or Ranchhodrai, the one who left the battlefield, and devotees tell the story of the chase to Muchukunda's cave as part of that name's meaning; Muchukunda's prayer for nothing but Krishna is told in Bhagavata recitations as a picture of devotion that wants nothing back.

games.q: you're Muchukunda, just woken. Krishna offers you any boon you want. what do you ask?
o: nothing but to love him, at his feet.
to go back to sleep, undisturbed.
games.why: he turns down every boon. after a lifetime of chasing kingdoms, he asks only for shelter at Krishna's feet.

practice: Bring to mind what you usually ask for: health, a grade, a fix at home. Asking is allowed; let those wishes sit to one side for a minute. Then, like Muchukunda, ask for nothing at all.
If you pray, simply say a name you love, wanting only to be near; if you don't, sit with what you love most without wanting anything from it.

wordCard.voice: Ranchhod, the one who left the battlefield, a loving name for Krishna in Gujarat. Today, the chase into Muchukunda's cave, and a king who asked for nothing but Krishna.

orig.note: Gujarati and Hindi, written here in Devanagari: Ranchhod, explained by devotees as the one who left the battlefield, a loving name for Krishna in Gujarat.
